item.title: How to Apply for EU Funding: 7 Steps to Portal Submission
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to apply for EU funding in 7 steps: find a call, check eligibility, get a PIC, build a consortium and submit on the Funding & Tenders Portal by 17:00.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

How you apply for EU funding depends first on who manages the money. Centrally managed programmes such as Horizon Europe, the EIC, Digital Europe and the Innovation Fund take applications on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal. For ESF+ and most agricultural (CAP) money, you apply to an authority in your own country, using national forms and rules. This guide covers the Portal route in seven steps, then the national routes for ESF+ and CAP, and what changes after Horizon Europe ends in 2027.

Which option is right for you?

Choose your route based on who manages the money. Use the table below to find the first page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant, any organisation typeOne single-stage call where you can join as a partner, not as coordinatorPortal Calls for proposals search, filtered to "Open for submission"
SME or startup with an innovation to scaleEIC or SME-friendly callsEIC Grants 2026: 7 Open EU Calls for SMEs
University or research groupA Horizon Europe Pillar II topic (RIA/IA) inside a consortiumThe Horizon Europe work programme
NGO, training provider or local public body working on jobs or inclusionESF+ through your national managing authorityThe ESF+ in your country
Farmer or rural businessYour country's CAP Strategic PlanApproved 28 CAP Strategic Plans
Industrial decarbonisation projectInnovation FundInnovation Fund calls
Grant consultant who submits oftenSet up the Portal workspace (EU Login, 2FA, PIC) once, then track calls by programmePortal registration: PIC in 6 steps

On a small budget, start with the free help: your National Contact Point (NCP) and the Enterprise Europe Network. Both are covered under "Next steps".

How to Apply for EU Grants: The 7-Step Overview

Applying for EU grants takes seven stages: find a call, check eligibility, register (EU Login and PIC), prepare the proposal with templates, assemble partners, submit on the Portal, and track the evaluation. The Commission tells applicants to read the How to participate section and its Online Manual before starting. The Portal Online Manual covers the whole grant lifecycle.

The table below gives each stage, the official page to use and the deadline that applies to it.

#StageOfficial pageDeadline or timing
1Find a callCalls for proposalsThe topic page shows the deadline date
2Check eligibilityThe topic conditions and the programme's General AnnexesBefore you write anything
3RegisterEU Login, then the Participant Register for a PICBefore you create the draft, because the coordinator's PIC is needed in the submission wizard (SEP manual)
4Prepare the proposalTemplates downloaded inside the submission systemPlan for several weeks
5Build the consortiumPortal Partner Search, NCPs, EENPartners need PICs before submission
6SubmitPortal Submission System17:00 Brussels time on the deadline day (Digital Europe guidance)
7Track the evaluationMy ProposalsHorizon Europe: result about 5 months after the deadline, grant signature about 8 months after (REA)

Stage 7 has fixed legal limits in Horizon Europe. Article 31 of Regulation (EU) 2021/695 gives the Commission a maximum of 5 months to inform applicants and 8 months to sign grant agreements, both counted from the submission deadline. For two-stage calls, first-stage results come about 3 months after the first deadline (HRB summary). Plan your cash flow with this in mind. If you submit in spring, money will not arrive before the following year.

Where to Find Open EU Funding Calls

You find open EU funding calls with the Funding & Tenders Portal search. You can filter it by programme, submission status and keyword. Calls for ESF+ and CAP do not appear there in full, because national authorities publish them.

The Portal search works like this (Online Manual: Find a call; ISED walkthrough):

  1. Open the Portal. In the Funding drop-down menu, click Calls for proposals.
  2. Under Programming period, choose 2021–2027.
  3. Under Programme, choose for example "Horizon Europe", "Digital Europe Programme" or "Innovation Fund".
  4. Under Submission status, tick Open for submission and Forthcoming. Forthcoming calls give you the most preparation time.
  5. Type a keyword into Quick search, for example "hydrogen", "soil" or "social inclusion". Use All filters to narrow by type of action.
  6. Open a topic. Its page lists the deadline, the budget, the type of action, eligibility conditions and the link into the submission system.

If you are logged in, the Portal can save your searches and send you its own email alerts. For calls where funded projects pass money on to third parties (cascade funding), see Cascade Funding Open Calls: Portal Filters and 2026 Dates.

Example: suppose you are an agri-tech startup. You could filter Programme = Horizon Europe, Submission status = Forthcoming and search "soil". That surfaces Cluster 6 topics from the 2026–2027 work programme before they open.

Common mistakes:

  • Reading a third-party summary of a call instead of the official topic page. Summaries leave out conditions. Always check the official topic text.
  • Treating "Closed" topics as useless. A closed topic often comes back in the next work programme in a similar form, so read it to prepare.
  • Looking for national ESF+ or CAP calls on the Portal. They are mostly not there (see the sections below).

Eligibility Checklist: Who Can Apply for EU Funding

Your eligibility depends on three things: your type of entity, the country you are established in, and whether the call requires a consortium. Every topic page lists its own conditions, and the work programme can override the default rules.

QuestionDefault rule (Horizon Europe example)Where to confirm
Are you a legal entity?Most calls require a registered legal entity. Individuals usually cannot applyTopic conditions
Where are you established?EU member states and Associated Countries are eligible for funding. Rules for third countries vary"List of participating countries" in the reference documents
How many partners are needed?RIA/IA: at least 3 independent legal entities from 3 different member states or Associated Countries, with at least one in a member state (FFG; KoWi)Topic text and General Annexes
Can you apply alone?Yes for some instruments, such as the EIC Accelerator for single SMEsTopic page
Is the money managed nationally?ESF+ and CAP: national rules applyYour managing authority

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Affiliated partners do not count as independent. Two subsidiaries of the same group, or three organisations in the same country, do not meet the three-country minimum (FFG). Fix: count your independent entities and their countries before you invite anyone else.
  • The topic text overrides the default. Some topics add extra conditions, such as a required type of partner or a limited set of countries. Fix: read the "Conditions" part of the topic page next to the General Annexes.
  • Non-EU organisations sometimes assume they get funded automatically. Being allowed to participate does not always mean being funded. Fix: check the participating countries list before you budget your role.

How to Apply for the European Social Fund (ESF+)

You apply for ESF+ through a managing authority in your own country or region, not through the central Portal. The only exception is the small EU-level EaSI strand. Calls, eligibility and co-financing are set nationally.

The numbers explain why. ESF+ has a budget of €142.7 billion for 2021–2027. About €142 billion of that runs under shared management by member states (€95.1 billion of it from the EU budget). The Commission-run EaSI strand has close to €762 million (fi-compass). Public bodies, private companies (especially small businesses), universities, associations and NGOs can all receive the national funding, but eligibility is decided "at the national and regional level in each country" (ESF+: how to access funding).

Steps for the national strand:

  1. Open The ESF+ in your country and choose your country.
  2. Read the national or regional ESF+ programme to see which priorities your project fits, such as youth employment, skills or social inclusion.
  3. Find the managing authority's contact details on that page, then go to its national ESF+ portal for open calls.
  4. Apply in the national system using the national forms and the national co-financing rules.

Steps for EaSI (EU-level):

  1. Check the annual work programme. The Commission says it is published in Q4 (ESF+).
  2. Search the Funding & Tenders Portal for EaSI calls and submit there, with a PIC, like any other centrally managed grant.

Example: in France, the official service-public.gouv.fr page describes the national ESF+ application procedure. Other countries have their own equivalents, linked from the ESF+ country pages.

The most common mistake is writing a Horizon-style proposal for an ESF+ call. National ESF+ calls use their own templates and scoring. Use the documents the managing authority provides.

EU Funding for Agriculture: Key Programmes to Know

EU funding for agriculture flows mainly through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), via national CAP Strategic Plans. For research-driven projects, there is also Horizon Europe's Cluster 6 (food, bioeconomy, natural resources, agriculture and environment).

ProgrammeWho it suitsHow you applyOfficial number
CAP Strategic Plans (EAGF and EAFRD)Farmers, rural businesses, producer groupsThrough the authority named in your country's plan28 plans; more than €307 billion of public spending for 2023–2027, including national co-financing (Commission factsheet)
Horizon Europe Cluster 6Universities, research centres, agri-tech SMEs in consortiaFunding & Tenders Portal€8.952 billion for 2021–2027 (FFG)
Innovation FundLarge-scale decarbonisation, including bio-based processesFunding & Tenders PortalIF25 Net-Zero Technologies call: €2.9 billion budget (Climate Action)

There are 28 plans because Belgium has two (Flanders and Wallonia) (approved plans list). So the first step is the same for every farmer: find your country's or region's plan and the measure that matches your investment. CAP payments do not run through Portal topics.

Choose by what you want to do. To fund farm investment or income support, go to CAP. To test a new method with research partners in several countries, go to Cluster 6. If you are an SME with a farming technology product, also read EIC Grants 2026: 7 Open EU Calls for SMEs.

One timing note: the CAP after 2027 is being negotiated as part of the next budget. The Council agreed its negotiating position on the future CAP on 26 October 2026. That is not final law, so do not plan around draft figures.

Post-Horizon Europe Climate Funding: What's Next

Horizon Europe runs until 2027. The Commission proposed a €175 billion successor (FP10) for 2028–2034, but as of October 2026 the next EU budget is not agreed. Climate funding continues meanwhile through the remaining Horizon Europe calls and the Innovation Fund.

What is confirmed (as of October 2026):

  • FP10 proposal. On 16 July 2025 the Commission proposed the 2028–2034 Framework Programme with a €175 billion budget (European Commission; House of Commons Library). It is linked to a proposed €409 billion European Competitiveness Fund, which would manage €68 billion of collaborative research (Science|Business).
  • Council position. Member states agreed a partial position on FP10 on 26 June 2026. Budget and horizontal issues were left out because they are tied to the wider budget negotiations.
  • No budget deal yet. EU leaders did not agree the 2028–2034 budget at their 15–16 October 2026 summit (Agence Europe). The Council timeline tracks progress.
  • The Innovation Fund is active now. The IF25 Net-Zero Technologies call closed on 23 April 2026 with 358 applications. On 19 October 2026 the Commission selected 77 projects for €3.4 billion in grants across 23 EEA countries (Climate Action). The call asked for €17.5 billion in total, about six times its €2.9 billion budget (ieu-monitoring).

Pitfalls:

  • Waiting for FP10. The 2026–2027 Horizon Europe work programmes still have deadlines. Ready projects should apply now instead of waiting for a programme whose budget and rules are still open.
  • Quoting draft structures as fact. Instrument names and budget shares in FP10 may change during negotiations. In a proposal, cite only adopted texts.
  • Underestimating competition. At six times oversubscribed, the Innovation Fund rewards mature, bankable projects. Early-stage ideas fit Horizon Europe or the EIC better.

Assembling a Consortium and Partners for Your Application

Many EU calls need a minimum number of independent partners from different eligible countries. For Horizon Europe RIA/IA, that is three from three countries. Use the Portal Partner Search, NCPs and the Enterprise Europe Network to find partners well before the deadline.

Steps:

  1. Set your gap list. From the topic's expected outcomes, write down the roles you cannot cover, for example "end-user pilot site in southern Europe" or "life-cycle assessment".
  2. Search the Portal. Use the Portal's Partner Search. You can search by keyword, geographic area or funding type. The results show organisation profiles, their past funded projects and contacts.
  3. Search the EEN database. The Enterprise Europe Network's Partnering Opportunities database is free and has profiles from more than 60 countries, including research cooperation requests (EEN Poland).
  4. Ask your NCP. The Horizon Europe NCP Portal lists NCP networks, and several of them run partner-search services.
  5. Collect PICs early. Every partner must be registered in the Participant Register with its own PIC (Online Manual). Send new partners the PIC registration guide.
  6. Agree the basics in writing. Before drafting, agree roles, budget shares and who coordinates.

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • A partner without a PIC in the last week. Validating a PIC takes time. Fix: make "PIC exists" a condition for joining.
  • Too many partners. Evaluators assess the capacity and role of each participant against the topic, not the number of partners, so a large consortium is not scored higher in itself (Online Manual). Fix: give every partner a role that clearly matches the topic's expected outcomes.
  • Spending budget on a partnership agreement too early. Under Horizon Europe, the costs of preparing the proposal and the consortium agreement are generally not eligible for funding (Annotated Grant Agreement). Fix: keep pre-award costs low.

Submitting Your Application on the Funding & Tenders Portal

To submit, you need EU Login access, a coordinator PIC, completed administrative forms (Part A) and the technical annex (Part B) uploaded as a PDF. The system closes automatically at 17:00 Brussels time on the deadline day. Late submissions are not accepted.

The sequence below follows the Proposal Submission Service user manual:

  1. Log in with EU Login. Two-factor authentication is required; see EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026.
  2. Open the topic page and click Start submission.
  3. Create the draft. Enter the coordinator's PIC (Step 3 of the wizard) plus the proposal acronym and short summary.
  4. Under Step 4, manage participants by adding each partner's PIC and contact persons.
  5. Edit the online Part A forms. Download the Part B template from inside the system. Do not use an old copy from a previous call.
  6. Upload Part B and any other annexes as PDFs. Multiple documents such as CVs must be merged into one PDF of up to 10 MB (Proposal Submission Service user manual).
  7. Click Validate. This checks the whole draft and shows errors and warnings, including missing fields and page or file problems.
  8. Click Submit. The system combines everything into one document and creates an e-receipt with the date and time. All coordinator contact persons get a confirmation email.
  9. Until the deadline, you can still update, download or withdraw the proposal. Each new submission replaces the previous one.

For guidance on writing Part B against the evaluation criteria, see Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map.

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Submitting at 16:55. Upload problems at the last minute cannot be fixed. Fix: submit a complete version at least 48 hours early, then resubmit improvements. Re-uploading before the deadline has no limit.
  • Going over the page limit. Excess pages may not be evaluated (Online Manual). Fix: check the limit on the topic page and run Validate after every upload.
  • "Validate" passing and no submission made. Validating does not submit. Fix: check that the status in My Proposals shows Submitted. See My Proposals: Status Table.

Next steps

You can do the next steps yourself today. Free public help is available if you get stuck, and paid consultants are an option if you would rather hand the work over.

Do this today:

  1. Open the Portal Calls for proposals page. Set Submission status to Forthcoming and Open for submission, filter by your programme, and save two or three topics that match your project.
  2. Check whether your organisation already has a PIC. If not, start registering now using the PIC guide.
  3. If your project is about jobs, skills or farming, open your country's ESF+ page or CAP Strategic Plan instead, and write down the managing authority's contact.

If you would rather not do it yourself:

  • National Contact Points (free as of October 2026; check the official page). Each country's NCPs give free advice on Horizon Europe calls and eligibility, and sometimes partner search (NCP Portal). This suits first-time applicants who need someone to check their topic choice. It does not suit people who want someone to write the proposal: NCPs advise, they do not draft.
  • Enterprise Europe Network (free as of October 2026; check the official page). It is a good fit for SMEs looking for partners through the partnering database. It is less useful for academic consortia that already have research networks.
  • Private grant consultants (paid). There is no official EU price list. Each firm sets its own fees, often a fixed fee, a success fee or both, so get a written quote that says who owns the text. Consultants suit companies with no time to write but a strong project. They do not suit very early ideas. One limitation: under Horizon Europe, proposal-preparation costs are generally not eligible for reimbursement (Annotated Grant Agreement), so you pay these fees from your own budget even if you win.

FAQ

How to apply for EU grants as a first-time applicant?

Start as a partner in someone else's consortium rather than as coordinator. You still need EU Login and a PIC, but the coordinator handles the submission. Ask your National Contact Point to check that your chosen topic fits before you commit time to it. Read the topic's conditions and the General Annexes before you write anything.

Can non-EU countries apply for EU funding agriculture programmes?

CAP support is paid through the member states' CAP Strategic Plans, so it is for beneficiaries in the EU. Horizon Europe Cluster 6 is different: entities from Associated Countries can be funded, and some third-country entities can take part depending on the participating countries list and the topic text. Always check whether participation actually comes with funding.

What happens to Horizon Europe projects after the programme ends in 2027?

Grants signed under Horizon Europe run for their full contracted duration, including after 2027, under their grant agreements. New calls from 2028 are expected under FP10, which the Commission proposed with €175 billion. Its final budget and rules depend on the 2028–2034 budget negotiations, which were still open in October 2026.

Do NGOs need a PIC number to apply through the European Social Fund?

For national ESF+ calls, the managing authority decides what registration you need, and that is usually a national system rather than the PIC. For EU-level EaSI calls submitted on the Funding & Tenders Portal, you need a PIC like any other Portal applicant. Check the call documents for which strand you are applying under.

item.title: Horizon Europe CSA Proposal Template: 7 Differences From RIA
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Horizon Europe CSA proposal template vs RIA: a section-by-section map of what changes in the 25-page CSA Part B, the 100% funding rate, TRL and impact.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The Horizon Europe CSA proposal template uses the same three Part B sections as the RIA template (Excellence, Impact, Implementation), but it has a shorter page limit: 25 pages, or 28 for lump-sum topics, against 40 and 45 for RIA/IA under the 2026–2027 forms (NCP Flanders). The other big differences are in what the sections ask for. In a CSA, Excellence is judged on the "quality of the proposed coordination and/or support measures" rather than how far you go beyond the state of the art. TRL, SSH integration and sex/gender analysis are not required. Funding is up to 100% for every type of organisation. Always download the template from your topic's own submission system, because the version attached to your call is the one that counts (criteri.ai).

Which option is right for you?

Start from your situation. The table below tells you which template version and which page to open first.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, first CSA, no PIC yetRegister your organisation, then download the CSA template from the topicPIC registration guide
You've written RIAs before and are switching to a CSAMap your RIA habits onto the 25-page CSA form, starting with the 7-difference table belowRIA 40-page section map
Writing proposals is part of your regular job (consultant, grants office)The 2026–2027 template (v5.x) plus the HE CSA evaluation form, used as your checklistPart B scoring map
Two-stage CSA topicThe "HE CSA stage 1" form: only Excellence and Impact are scored, with a threshold of 4 eachHE CSA stage 1 form
Small budget, SME or NGO that wants to re-grant moneyA CSA topic with financial support to third parties, or apply to someone else's cascade callCascade funding open calls
Lump-sum CSA topicThe lump-sum variant (28 pages) and a detailed budget tableYour topic page → "Topic conditions and documents"

Why these picks: beginners get stuck on registration before they ever reach the template. RIA veterans tend to overwrite Excellence. Two-stage applicants who use the full form waste pages on Implementation, which isn't scored at stage 1 (HE CSA evaluation form).

What Is a CSA in Horizon Europe (Coordination and Support Action)?

A CSA (Coordination and Support Action) pays for coordination, networking, dissemination and policy support. It does not pay for original research the way an RIA or IA does. EMDESK describes CSAs as actions that "do not fund research or innovation" and instead facilitate cooperation, capacity building, knowledge dissemination and policy support (EMDESK). The binding definitions are in the Work Programme General Annexes (General Annexes 2026–2027) and the Horizon Europe Programme Guide.

Typical CSA work includes stakeholder workshops, standardisation, strategy and roadmap development, and aligning national and European priorities (EMDESK). Some CSAs also re-grant money to third parties. Examples from 2026–2027 topics include caps of EUR 60,000 per third party in some research-infrastructure and EIC ecosystem topics, and EUR 750,000 per third party in a cross-domain open science topic (Work Programme 2026–2027, Annex III).

Who can apply also differs from RIA. Standard RIA/IA consortia need at least three independent legal entities from three different countries, at least one of them in a Member State. CSA applications "may be submitted by one or more legal entities," so a single organisation can apply unless the topic says otherwise (General Annexes). Entities from non-associated third countries can join CSAs as associated partners unless the topic excludes this.

Example (from a real 2026 topic): the EIC Scaling Club 2.0 call (HORIZON-EIC-2026-BAS-02-SCALEUP) was a CSA with a EUR 4 million budget and one expected grant. Its deadline was 25 June 2026. It had to support at least 70 deep-tech companies through networking and learning, at least 35 of them from the EIC portfolio (EIC). There is no lab work and no prototype. The deliverables are a support programme and its reach.

CSA vs RIA: What Sections Are Different in the Proposal Template?

Both templates use the same Part B skeleton (1 Excellence, 2 Impact, 3 Quality and efficiency of implementation). What differs is the page budget, the wording of the criteria and several sub-elements. Here are the seven differences that change how you write:

#ElementRIA template (2026–2027)CSA template (2026–2027)
1Total page limit40 pages (45 lump sum)25 pages (28 lump sum) (NCP Flanders)
2Excellence criterionObjectives "ambitious, and go beyond the state-of-the-art"; soundness of methodology"Clarity and pertinence of the project's objectives" and "Quality of the proposed coordination and/or support measures including soundness of methodology" (HE CSA evaluation form)
3Section 1.2 title"Methodology""Coordination and/or support measures and methodology" (HE CSA form)
4TRLStart and end TRL stated in 1.1 where relevant (proposia)Not applicable (Enspire Science)
5SSH integration, sex/gender analysisRequired sub-elements of 1.2 (about 0.5 and 1 page)"This aspect is not required for a CSA type of project" (Enspire Science)
6Funding rate100% for all beneficiaries (IA: 70% for profit-making entities)Up to 100% for all beneficiaries (General Annexes)
7Minimum applicants3 independent entities, 3 countries1 or more legal entities

Some things are the same in both templates. In 2026–2027 the "scale and significance" guidance was dropped from section 2.1, the 2.3 summary became optional, and the tables for "other cost categories" and "in-kind contributions" were removed from 3.1 (NCP Flanders; Accelopment). The scoring thresholds also match: at least 3 per criterion and 10 overall for single-stage proposals (HE CSA evaluation form). If you want the RIA side page by page, see the RIA 40-page section map.

Pitfalls when converting an RIA draft into a CSA:

  • Pasting a state-of-the-art review into 1.1. Evaluators score the pertinence of your objectives, not novelty. Keep the context to a few paragraphs on the gap your coordination fills. Evaluators do still sometimes comment on state-of-the-art awareness in CSA reports (proposia), so show you know the field without turning it into a literature review.
  • Using an old 30-page template. The pre-2026 CSA limit was 30 pages (33 lump sum) (Accelopment). Pages beyond the limit are not considered by evaluators, so download a fresh copy.
  • Keeping empty RIA headings such as "Gender dimension in research content" with "N/A" under them. Just follow the CSA headings.

How Is the Funding Rate Different for CSA Proposals?

CSAs are funded at up to 100% of eligible costs for every type of organisation. In an IA, by contrast, profit-making beneficiaries get 70% (General Annexes). RIAs are also at 100% for all beneficiaries, so for a university the RIA and CSA rates are the same. The gap only matters to companies that compare a CSA with an IA.

Action typeUniversity / NGO / public bodyCompany (incl. SME)Indirect costs
RIA100%100%25% flat rate
IA100%70%25% flat rate
CSA100%100%25% flat rate

Rates as of October 2026 (criteri.ai summary of the General Annexes and MGA). A topic can set a different rate in its conditions, so the 100% is a maximum and not a guarantee (General Annexes).

The flat 25% for indirect costs is where CSA budgets often go wrong. It applies to eligible direct costs excluding subcontracting and financial support to third parties (criteri.ai). CSAs often subcontract venues, translation or event logistics, and they often re-grant money. None of that earns overhead.

Example (illustrative numbers): a CSA plans EUR 600,000 in personnel, EUR 150,000 in travel and other goods, EUR 200,000 in subcontracted event organisation and EUR 1,000,000 in third-party grants. Indirect costs are 25% × (600,000 + 150,000) = EUR 187,500. The subcontracting and the third-party grants add nothing to that figure. If you had planned overheads on the full EUR 1.95 million, you would be EUR 300,000 short.

What Goes in the 'Excellence' Section of a CSA Proposal?

The CSA Excellence section is scored on clear, pertinent objectives and on the quality of your coordination and support measures. Scientific novelty and advances beyond the state of the art are not scored (HE CSA evaluation form). Section 1.2 asks you to "describe and explain the coordination and/or support measures and the overall methodology, including the concepts, models and assumptions that underpin your work," to explain how this delivers your objectives, and to name challenges in the chosen methodology (HE CSA form).

For the pre-2026 30-page CSA form, Enspire Science's analysis recommended about 2 pages for 1.1 and 6 pages for 1.2 (4 for the core measures and methodology, 2 for other elements), compared with 4 and 15 for RIA/IA (Enspire Science). With 25 pages in 2026–2027, check the indicative allocations printed in your template rather than reusing those numbers.

Steps to draft it:

  1. Open your topic on the Funding & Tenders Portal. Under Topic conditions and documents, read the "Expected outcome" and "Scope" text and copy every expected outcome into a scratch list.
  2. In 1.1 Objectives and ambition, write 3–6 objectives, and have each one name the outcome it serves. Make them measurable in coordination terms (number of Member States aligned, number of stakeholders engaged, roadmap adopted by a named body).
  3. Under ambition, explain why this coordination is needed now, for example fragmented national programmes or missing standards. Leave out TRL claims.
  4. In 1.2 Coordination and/or support measures and methodology, separate the concept (why this mix of measures works) from the method (how you'll run each one). Enspire recommends this split even though the CSA template blurs it (Enspire Science).
  5. List each measure type, such as mapping study, mutual-learning workshops, an open call for third parties or policy briefs. For each, give its target group, its format and how you will select participants.
  6. End 1.2 with the methodological challenges you see (low attendance, no buy-in from ministries) and how you'll handle them. The template asks for this explicitly.

Example (illustrative): for a topic asking for "better alignment of national circular-economy funding programmes," a weak objective reads "Promote cooperation among funders." A stronger one reads "Bring at least 12 national funding agencies to agree a joint call roadmap by month 24, adopted in a signed memorandum." The second version gives evaluators something they can score under "clarity and pertinence."

Open science practices are mandatory across Horizon Europe in general, but the CSA template does not ask for the dedicated open-science research-output plan found in RIA 1.2 (Enspire Science). If your CSA produces datasets (for example a stakeholder mapping database), say how you'll make them open, and check your template wording.

Do CSA Proposals Need to Show Own Resources or Co-financing?

Usually not. At a 100% funding rate there is no co-financing gap to cover from your own resources, and the 2026–2027 template no longer has the "in-kind contributions" table in section 3.1 (NCP Flanders). The co-financing question mostly belongs to IAs: a profit-making beneficiary funded at 70% covers the other 30% itself (criteri.ai). What counts as an eligible cost is set out in Article 6 of the Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement.

"100%" still doesn't mean every euro you spend is reimbursed. Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Ineligible costs. Anything outside the Article 6 eligibility rules (MGA) is paid by you, even at 100%. Fix: have your finance office check costs like hospitality, recoverable VAT and equipment depreciation before you finalise the budget.
  • Topic-specific rates. A topic can set a rate below 100% in its conditions (General Annexes). Fix: read the "Specific conditions" block on the topic page before planning anything.
  • Equipment justification. In 2026–2027, purchase costs only need justifying in 3.1 when equipment exceeds 15% of personnel costs (Accelopment). CSAs rarely buy equipment, so a large equipment line will look odd to evaluators.
  • Lump-sum CSAs. You still submit a detailed budget, but you are paid on completed work packages rather than on reported costs. Fix: use the lump-sum template (28 pages) and define work packages whose completion can be checked.

Is TRL (Technology Readiness Level) Required in a CSA Proposal?

No. TRL is not applicable to CSA proposals because CSAs don't develop technology (Enspire Science). In the RIA template, by contrast, 1.1 asks for start and end TRL where relevant (proposia). RIAs typically sit around TRL 2–5/6 and IAs around TRL 5–8 (EMDESK). The TRL scale itself is defined in the General Annexes.

Pitfalls:

  • Promising TRL progression in a CSA. Writing "we will advance the platform from TRL 4 to 6" suggests research or innovation work that a CSA isn't meant to fund. Evaluators may read it as a scope mismatch. Fix: describe what your measures change, such as access, alignment, skills or uptake.
  • Leaving maturity out completely when the topic is about technology uptake. Example (illustrative): a CSA that helps SMEs adopt results from earlier EU projects can say those results "come from completed IA pilots." That describes other people's work, which is fine. Just don't make TRL an objective of your project.

What Impact Section Content Is Expected in a CSA vs RIA?

CSA impact sections centre on stakeholder uptake, dissemination networks and policy or practice change. RIA impact sections are built around scientific results and their exploitation. The sub-sections are the same in both: 2.1 pathways, 2.2 measures to maximise impact, and an optional 2.3 summary. The criterion wording is also shared: "Credibility of the pathways to achieve the expected outcomes and impacts specified in the work programme" and "Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities" (HE CSA evaluation form).

Impact elementRIA emphasisCSA emphasis
Results you exploitData, methods, prototypes, publicationsRoadmaps, policy briefs, networks, trained people, joint calls
Main "users"Researchers, industry, follow-up projectsMinistries, funders, agencies, standards bodies, sector associations
IP strategy in 2.2Patents, licences, background/foreground IPUsually light: open licences for guides and reports
Barriers to name in 2.1Technical, market, regulatoryPolitical buy-in, stakeholder fatigue, keeping the network going after the project
Scale and significanceRemoved as a required breakdown in 2026–2027Removed as a required breakdown in 2026–2027 (NCP Flanders)

For RIA, the 2026–2027 template cut the pathways allocation from 4 to 3 pages (Accelopment). CSA pages are tighter still, so a compact table usually does more work than prose.

Example (illustrative 2.1 entry): Outcome from the topic: "Funders coordinate calls." Your result: "Joint call roadmap." Pathway: "Roadmap presented to the national funders' board at month 20, followed by a signed memorandum at month 24." Barrier: "Election cycles in two countries." Mitigation: "Engage agency-level staff as well as political representatives."

For the ranking, CSA and RIA criteria are weighted equally. The 1.5 weighting of Impact for ranking applies to Innovation Actions (General Annexes). For how each sub-criterion turns into a score, see the Part B scoring map.

How to Write the Implementation Section for a CSA Proposal?

In section 3, the work packages should be the coordination engine itself: mapping, events, mutual learning, third-party calls and dissemination. Management and governance should be visible in their own work package. This section gives you no room to rebuild an RIA-style methodology. The award criterion is the same for every action type: quality and effectiveness of the work plan, allocation of resources, and the capacity and role of each participant (HE CSA evaluation form). The 2026–2027 form removed the 3.1 tables on other cost categories and in-kind contributions (NCP Flanders).

Steps:

  1. Draft the WP list first. Example structure (illustrative): WP1 Management, WP2 Mapping and baseline, WP3 Mutual learning and events, WP4 Open call for third parties (only if the topic allows it), WP5 Roadmap and policy recommendations, WP6 Communication, dissemination and sustainability.
  2. Give each WP measurable deliverables: event reports with attendance, a database, a roadmap or a policy brief. Use milestones for decisions, such as "Open call launched" or "Roadmap endorsed."
  3. Fill in the risk table with coordination risks, for example low participation, partner drop-out or a delayed political endorsement, each with a mitigation.
  4. Justify effort per partner. CSAs are mostly person-months, so show why each partner's months match its role: who chairs which working group and who runs which country's outreach.
  5. In 3.2 Capacity of participants, show networks rather than research track records: members, existing mandates, past events of a similar size.
  6. If a single entity applies (allowed for CSAs), explain how you'll reach stakeholders across countries without consortium partners, for example through associated partners or subcontracted national hubs. Remember that subcontracting earns no 25% overhead.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • A "research" WP with experiments or surveys sold as studies. Fix: frame them as mapping or analysis that feeds coordination. If the topic really needs new research, it's probably the wrong action type for you.
  • Communication bundled into management. Fix: give dissemination its own WP so evaluators can see it under Impact too.
  • No plan for after the project. Fix: add a sustainability deliverable, for example a network charter or a hand-over to an existing association.
  • An open call without selection rules. Topics that allow financial support to third parties may require independent review and grants as the only form of support (Work Programme 2026–2027, Annex III). Fix: describe the eligibility rules, evaluation, maximum amounts and conflict-of-interest handling.

Exact UI path to get the right template:

  1. On the Funding & Tenders Portal, search the topic ID and open the topic page.
  2. Under Topic conditions and documents, open Standard application form (HE CSA) and the matching evaluation form to read them.
  3. Click Start submission, sign in with your EU Login (two-factor guide), select the organisation by PIC and create the draft.
  4. In the submission system, use Download Part B templates. This is the version bound to your call.
  5. Upload the finished PDF and click Validate before Submit. You can then track the proposal in My Proposals.

Next steps

Things you can do today:

  1. Open your target topic, check the Type of action says CSA, and download the Part B template from the submission system rather than from an old shared drive.
  2. Copy the HE CSA evaluation form criteria into your draft as hidden headings, then delete anything you wrote that doesn't serve one of them, starting with TRL and state-of-the-art text.
  3. Recalculate indirect costs leaving out subcontracting and third-party support.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs). Every Member State and Associated Country has Horizon Europe NCPs, listed on the Funding & Tenders Portal NCP page. Their advice is generally free of charge (as of October 2026; check your national NCP). They suit first-time applicants and anyone who needs a rules check. They don't suit people who want someone to write the text: NCPs advise but won't draft your proposal, and their capacity before big deadlines is limited.
  • Private grant consultants. These suit organisations with a confirmed topic and little in-house writing time. Fees aren't published centrally and vary by firm and by model (fixed fee, success fee or both), so ask for a written quote and what's included (as of October 2026). They don't suit very small budgets, and a consultant can't make up for a weak consortium or a topic that doesn't fit. If you need technical help with the Portal itself, use the official helpdesk route.

FAQ

What is the difference between RIA and CSA in Horizon Europe?

An RIA funds research that creates new knowledge or tests new technology, typically at TRL 2–5/6. A CSA funds coordination, networking, dissemination and policy support without original research (EMDESK). The CSA template is shorter (25 vs 40 pages) and judges Excellence on the quality of the coordination measures. A CSA can also be submitted by a single legal entity.

Can a CSA include research activities?

As a rule, no. CSAs are for coordination and support, and research and innovation activities belong in RIAs and IAs (EMDESK). Mapping studies or analyses that feed coordination are normal. If the topic's expected outcomes need new scientific results, check the General Annexes and the topic text, or look for an RIA topic instead.

What is the funding rate for CSA Horizon Europe?

Up to 100% of eligible costs for all beneficiaries, plus a 25% flat rate for indirect costs on eligible direct costs other than subcontracting and financial support to third parties (criteri.ai). A topic can set a different rate in its specific conditions (General Annexes).

Where can I download the Horizon Europe CSA proposal template?

The reference copy is the "Standard application form (HE CSA)" linked from each CSA topic page under Topic conditions and documents (HE CSA form). The editable Part B you actually submit comes from Download Part B templates inside the submission system after Start submission. Use that one, because the version tied to your call is the one that applies (criteri.ai).

item.title: EU Funding and Tenders Portal Participant Register: 5 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How the EU Funding and Tenders Portal Participant Register works: PIC vs register, the 6-step wizard, LEAR appointment, validation documents and role updates.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The EU Funding and Tenders Portal Participant Register is the part of the Portal where your organisation is registered, given its PIC (Participant Identification Code) and later validated. It is also where your LEAR and other authorised users are managed. You need a 9-digit PIC to submit a proposal (Online Manual). Getting from zero to grant-ready takes five steps: search for an existing PIC, register, pass legal validation, appoint a LEAR, and assign the signatory roles.

Which option is right for you?

Pick your situation from the table below. Each row tells you what to do first and which page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to openWhy
First-time applicant (startup, NGO, researcher)Search for a PIC, then register only if nothing turns upHow to Participate > Participant Register > Search a PICMany organisations, or one of their departments, are already registered
University or large institutionFind the central PIC your research office already managesSearch a PIC, then contact your grants officeA department registering its own PIC creates a duplicate
Proposal approved, invitation to grant preparation receivedAnswer the Central Validation Service and appoint the LEARMy Organisations > Actions > View organisation detailsYou can't sign the grant until both are validated
Daily grant management (several projects)Ask the LEAR to add Account Administrators, LSIGNs and FSIGNsMy Organisations > Actions > Edit RolesThe LEAR can't sign everything personally
Tight budget, no consultantDo it yourself with the Online Manual and the IT HelpdeskOnline Manual > Registration and validationRegistration and validation cost nothing
Consultant registering for a clientRegister the client as a backup Self-registrant, never with your own company dataRegistration wizard, "Define authorised users" stepThe client's legal representative must still appoint the client's LEAR

If you only want the PIC basics, see our step-by-step guide EU Funding and Tenders Portal Registration: PIC in 6 Steps. The rest of this guide covers what happens after the PIC is created.

What is the Participant Register and how is it different from a PIC?

The Participant Register is your organisation's full profile in the Funding & Tenders Portal. The PIC is just the 9-digit ID created when that profile is registered. You need both to apply. The register holds your legal data, contacts, documents, financial capacity results and user roles. The PIC is the key you type into a proposal so the system can pull all of that in (Online Manual).

People mix them up because the PIC appears straight away, at the end of the wizard. A freshly created PIC is provisional (not yet validated), though. It lets you apply, but it doesn't let you sign a grant (Online Manual, Registration and validation).

PICParticipant Register
What it is9-digit identification codeDatabase record and management area for the organisation
When you get itImmediately when the registration wizard finishesCreated at the same moment, then filled in over time
Enough to submit a proposal?YesNot needed beyond registration
Enough to sign a grant?No, it must be validated firstMust contain the validated legal data, a validated LEAR and (if requested) a financial capacity assessment
Who manages itNobody "manages" a codeSelf-registrant before validation, then the LEAR and Account Administrators
Where you see itProposal forms, Search a PICMy Organisations in the Portal's "Manage My Area"

Example: A small biotech startup registers on Monday and copies the PIC into a Horizon Europe proposal on Tuesday. Nobody checks its legal documents at that stage. The Central Validation Service only asks for them if the proposal is selected. Validation happens after evaluation results, and only for beneficiaries, affiliated entities and contractors. Associated partners and subcontractors don't need it (Online Manual).

Common mistakes:

  • "We have a PIC, so we're done." You still need validation and a LEAR. Without a LEAR you can't update legal entity data or sign contracts electronically (Online Manual).
  • Assuming the PIC is the only identifier you'll ever need. Check your call document. If it asks for a different organisation identifier, use the code it asks for.

How to register an organisation in the Participant Register

You register an organisation once, through the "Register your organisation" wizard, signed in with EU Login. You'll need the legal name, VAT or registration number, address and legal form. If you have your official documents in front of you while you fill it in, you're less likely to declare something (legal form, non-profit, public/private) that later fails validation (Online Manual).

Before you start

  1. Create or sign in to an EU Login account. Two-factor authentication is now part of signing in. If it blocks you, see EU Funding and Tenders Portal Two Factor Authentication 2026.
  2. Go to How to Participate > Participant Register > Search a PIC and search for several spellings of your name, so you don't create a duplicate (Online Manual).
  3. Have these at hand: your company registry extract, VAT certificate (or proof of VAT exemption), statutes, and the founding act if you're a public body.

The wizard, step by step

The current IT guide describes these screens (IT How To, Registration steps):

  1. Provide organisation identification details. Enter the Legal name, VAT number and Registration country. For EU countries the VAT number is checked against databases. A warning icon appears if the VAT number isn't found or the legal name doesn't match.
  2. Check the duplicate list. The system shows "possible duplicates based on the provided Legal name and registration country." Click Use this PIC if your organisation is listed. Click Continue registration only if it's really not there.
  3. Provide organisation data. Enter the main contact details and the official language. If your VAT was validated but the address is different, a mismatch message appears. Fix it now, not later.
  4. Provide legal information. Choose the Legal form from the dropdown. Fill in the optional extra fields if they apply to you.
  5. Define authorised users. Your EU Login becomes the main authorised user, with the Self-registrant role. You can add a backup authorised user, which is a good idea if you're a consultant or might leave the organisation.
  6. Summary. Check everything. Use Edit to correct entries and Print to keep a copy.
  7. Success. Your PIC is displayed. Continue to update takes you to the data update screens.

You can save a draft after the organisation data page and pick it up later under My Organisations > Continue Registration. Unfinished drafts are deleted after one year (Online Manual). Once a PIC exists, the wizard can't be run again for that organisation. Every later change goes through data updates (IT How To, Participant register).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Registering as an individual. Natural persons can register, but some labels don't fit. The manual tells you to use your country of residence instead of the country of registration, and your passport number instead of a registration number (Online Manual).
  • Using a trading name. Enter the legal name exactly as it appears in the registry extract. A mismatch is one of the first things validation flags.
  • Ticking "non-profit" or "public body" because it feels right. You'll have to prove that status with statutes or a founding act. Only declare it if those documents say so.

How to appoint a LEAR (Legal Entity Appointed Representative)

Once the Central Validation Service asks for it, the Self-registrant enters the LEAR's details in the Portal. The system then generates an appointment letter. Your legal representative signs it, and you upload it with both people's ID and proof of the representative's authority. The LEAR appointment is mandatory for every validated participant (Online Manual, LEAR appointment and validation).

Most PIC guides stop before this step, and it's usually what delays grant signature. Here is the official sequence:

  1. Wait for the notification. The Central Validation Service contacts the Self-registrant, the person who registered the organisation, to start the LEAR procedure. Validating the organisation comes first: it's a prerequisite for validating the LEAR (H2020 Online Manual).
  2. Choose two people. You need the LEAR, who will handle daily administration, and the legal representative, who has authority to bind the organisation and will appoint the LEAR.
  3. Enter the data. Go to My Organisations > Actions > View organisation details > Authorised users/Lear section > Add Lear. Enter the LEAR's name and contact details and the legal representative's details (Online Manual).
  4. Download the generated LEAR appointment letter. It lists the LEAR's roles and duties and includes consent to the Portal Terms and Conditions.
  5. Sign it. The legal representative dates and signs the letter, either by hand in ink or with a qualified electronic signature (QES) under the eIDAS Regulation (Online Manual).
  6. Upload three items: the signed letter; copies of valid ID for both the legal representative and the LEAR (photo and signature pages); and a document proving the legal representative's authority that shows their function and names them, such as statutes, a board decision or a registry extract.
  7. Activate the account. After validation the LEAR gets an email with activation instructions or a PIN code by SMS. If the PIN doesn't work, call the IT Helpdesk on +32 (0)2 299 2222 (Online Manual).

Keep the original signed documents. The manual says you must keep them for controls and audits.

Example (illustrative): At a mid-sized NGO, the executive director is the legal representative under the statutes. The grants officer becomes the LEAR. The director signs the letter with a QES, and the officer uploads the letter, both IDs and the statutes page naming the director's powers. If the statutes only say "the Board" represents the NGO, the officer also uploads the board resolution appointing the director. Without that link in the chain, the reviewer can't see why this person had authority to sign.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • The legal representative appoints themselves as LEAR. This is allowed, but the LEAR handles routine admin work. Most organisations choose someone in the grants office.
  • The proof of authority doesn't name the signatory. A generic statute clause isn't enough on its own. Add a document that names the person.
  • A scanned QES. A printed and re-scanned e-signature is no longer a qualified signature. Upload the original signed PDF, or sign in ink.

How does organisation validation work and how long does it take?

The Central Validation Service, run by the Research Executive Agency (REA), compares your uploaded documents with what you declared and then marks the PIC as validated. Validation only starts when you're selected for funding. It happens once and is reused for all later EU grants and tenders (REA Central Validation Service presentation).

How it runs:

  1. You receive an evaluation result letter or invitation to grant preparation.
  2. The Central Validation Service contacts the Self-registrant through the Participant Register (Online Manual).
  3. You upload the requested documents and answer questions about legal personality and any special status: non-profit, public/private, international organisation.
  4. The PIC is validated, followed by the LEAR appointment.
  5. If the call requires it, a financial capacity assessment follows. Coordinators also have bank account validation (Online Manual).

How long it takes: The Online Manual doesn't publish a fixed processing time (as of October 2026). The REA's guidance points to two things that actually set the pace: how quickly you answer, and whether your documents match what you declared. In practice, an organisation whose registry extract, VAT record and declared data all match is a simple case. Branches, recently merged entities and entities with an unusual legal form usually need extra rounds of questions. Plan around your grant preparation deadline rather than an assumed number of days.

The rule that catches most people out: all communication with the Central Validation Service has to go through the Participant Register (the My Organisations page). Emails and other channels are not accepted (Online Manual). If a request lands while the Self-registrant is on holiday, the backup Self-registrant you added in the wizard can answer it.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • The Self-registrant has left the organisation. Nobody can see the requests. Fix: ask the IT Helpdesk to help add a new authorised user. Our guide EU Funding and Tenders Portal Helpdesk: Ticket in 5 Steps shows how to file the ticket.
  • Watching the proposal status instead of the organisation messages. Grant preparation and validation run side by side. Check your status in My Proposals and check the PIC's messages too.

What documents are needed for validation (legal entity and financial capacity)?

Legal validation needs a Legal Entity Form plus official proof of your legal name, legal form, address and VAT status. A financial capacity assessment needs your recent accounts, but it's only requested when the grant amount and your entity type call for one. The two checks are separate and use different documents.

Legal entity validation

According to the REA and the earlier Online Manual, you'll need:

Entity typeDocuments
All entitiesLegal Entity Form (LEF), completed, dated and signed (stamped where applicable)
Private companies, SMEs, startupsOfficial registry extract plus VAT registration document, or proof of VAT exemption
Public bodiesThe law, decree or decision that established the body, plus VAT document
Non-profit organisationsStatutes showing the non-profit status, plus registration and VAT documents
International organisationsThe treaty or founding act
Natural personsValid ID or passport, plus VAT document if applicable

Sources: H2020 Online Manual, Validation of organisation; REA Central Validation Service.

How old the documents can be: The H2020 manual said VAT documents and registry extracts "cannot be older than 6 months." More recent REA presentations allow extracts and VAT documents under one year old (REA presentation). Because the sources disagree, the safe option is to upload an extract issued within the last six months. Documents in any official EU language are accepted, and an English translation is recommended. Each uploaded file can be at most 6 MB (Online Manual, Data updates).

SME status: If being an SME is an eligibility condition, the Portal asks you to complete an SME self-assessment when you don't have one from the last two years. You enter figures from your last approved accounting period (Online Manual). For SME-specific calls, see EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify.

Financial capacity assessment

The Online Manual says financial capacity is assessed for beneficiaries and affiliated entities, with these exceptions: public bodies, international organisations, individual grant requests of EUR 60,000 or less, and programmes with their own rules (Online Manual, Financial capacity assessment). In Horizon Europe the check is "normally" done only for the coordinator, and only when the requested amount is EUR 500,000 or more (Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, General Annexes).

  • Documents: usually profit and loss accounts and balance sheets for the last two closed financial years, a business plan, and an audit report from an approved external auditor where one exists.
  • Where to upload: My Organisations > Actions > View organisation details > Financial capacity.
  • How it's judged: liquidity, financial autonomy, solvency and profitability, plus dependency on EU funding and past deficits or revenue.
  • What happens if it's weak: the measures include joint and several liability, prefinancing in instalments, a prefinancing guarantee, no prefinancing, replacing the partner, or rejection (Online Manual).

An assessment stays valid for 18 months after the close of the most recent accounting period it covered (REA presentation).

Example (illustrative): A two-year-old startup coordinating a EUR 600,000 Horizon Europe grant has only one closed financial year. It uploads that year's accounts and a business plan. If the result is weak, it should expect measures such as a prefinancing guarantee rather than automatic rejection. For EIC calls, check the programme's own rules. See EIC Accelerator Deadlines 2026.

What roles exist in the Participant Register besides LEAR?

Besides the LEAR, an organisation can have a Self-registrant, Account Administrators, Legal Signatories (LSIGN), Financial Signatories (FSIGN), a Primary Audit Contact and Audit Contacts. Each role is linked to an EU Login account (Online Manual, Roles and access rights).

RoleAssigned byWhat it can doHow many
LEARValidated by the Central Validation ServiceUpdate organisation data; nominate and revoke signatories and Account Administrators; see all proposals and projectsOne per organisation
Self-registrantTakes the role automatically by registeringProvide information and documents until the LEAR is validatedAs set in the wizard
Account AdministratorLEARCarry out tasks the LEAR delegatesUnlimited
LSIGN (Legal Signatory)LEAR or Account AdministratorSign grant agreements and amendments, once assigned to a projectAs needed
FSIGN (Financial Signatory)LEAR or Account AdministratorSign financial statements and cost claims, once assigned to a projectAs needed
PAuCo (Primary Audit Contact)Given to the LEAR automaticallyNominate audit contactsOne
AuCo (Audit Contact)PAuCoHandle audit tasks and communication with EU auditorsAs needed

Signatories are nominated at organisation level first. The coordinator or the organisation then assigns them to individual projects through My Projects > Actions > Project Consortium (Online Manual, Data updates). When nominating a signatory, the LEAR can add a comment that limits the scope, such as "Horizon Europe projects only."

Example setup for a university (illustrative): The LEAR is the head of the research office. Two Account Administrators in that office handle routine role requests. The vice-rector for research is an LSIGN, and the finance director plus one deputy are FSIGNs. Faculty members don't hold organisation roles at all. They get project-level roles from the coordinator.

How to update or correct your organisation's data and roles after validation

Small corrections can be made in the Participant Register, but any change to legal data needs supporting documents and re-checking by the Central Validation Service. Replacing the LEAR means going through the appointment procedure again. After validation, only the LEAR and Account Administrators can make changes. Before validation, the Self-registrant can (Online Manual, Data updates).

Change organisation data

  1. Go to My Organisations > Actions > View organisation details > Edit Organisation Data. Older guides call this Actions > Modify Organisation.
  2. Edit the field, for example the legal address after a move.
  3. Upload the supporting document: a new registry extract, VAT certificate or board decision, each under 6 MB.
  4. Submit, then watch the organisation's messages for questions from the Central Validation Service.
  5. If you're in ongoing grants, ask your coordinator to tell the Project Officers. Changes such as partial or universal transfers of rights may also need grant amendments (Online Manual).

Change roles

  1. The LEAR or an Account Administrator opens My Organisations > Actions > Edit Roles.
  2. Add or revoke Account Administrators, LSIGNs and FSIGNs.
  3. Revoke access as soon as someone leaves. The manual warns that if grants or contracts are signed by people whose access should have been revoked, the organisation is responsible.

Replace the LEAR

Appoint the new LEAR using the same process as the first appointment, starting from Authorised users/Lears > Replace LEAR (Online Manual). You'll need a new letter signed by the current legal representative, new ID copies and new proof of authority. If only the LEAR's email address has changed, the Central Validation Service must be told through the same section.

Common mistake: waiting until the LEAR has already left. There is only one LEAR, so while that seat is empty nobody can change legal data. Start the replacement during the notice period.

How to find a lost or forgotten PIC

Use How to Participate > Participant Register > Search a PIC. Search for the full or partial legal name and filter by country before you think about registering again (Online Manual).

  1. Open Search a PIC and type part of the legal name. Try a few variants: with and without "GmbH"/"Ltd", the name in your national language, older names.
  2. Filter by country.
  3. Check under My Organisations while signed in. Every PIC where your EU Login holds a role is listed there.
  4. Search old proposal submission receipts or grant documents for a 9-digit number.
  5. Universities and hospitals: ask the research or grants office. Departments should use the central PIC.

If you find out you have two PICs, don't keep using both. Report the duplicate to the Central Validation Service through Portal messaging in the Participant Register (Online Manual). Keep the PIC with the most validated history, which will usually be the older one.

Next steps

For the formal rules behind every check in this guide, read the Commission's Rules for Legal Entity Validation, LEAR Appointment and Financial Capacity Assessment. The Online Manual pages tell you which screens to use. The Rules document is the reference to check when your case doesn't fit the standard pattern.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs) for Horizon Europe are free, government-funded advisers in each country. They're good for first-time applicants with procedural questions. They won't fill in the Portal for you, and how much time they can give varies by country (as of October 2026; check your NCP's page).
  • Enterprise Europe Network advisers are also free and aimed at SMEs. They're less suited to universities, whose research offices usually handle this already.
  • Private grant consultants can act as backup Self-registrant and prepare documents. Fees vary widely and are set by each firm, either fixed or tied to success, so ask for a written quote. They're useful if you're applying under time pressure. They're not for you if you just want a PIC, since that's free. And they can't replace your legal representative's signature or act as your LEAR.

Related guides on this site:

FAQ

What is a PIC number in the EU Funding and Tenders Portal?

A PIC (Participant Identification Code) is the 9-digit code your organisation gets when it finishes the Participant Register wizard. You enter it in proposals so the Portal can pull in your organisation's data. It starts out unvalidated. It's validated only if you're selected for funding.

Who can act as LEAR for a university or NGO?

Any person the legal representative appoints can be the LEAR. Usually it's someone in the research office or grants department, not the rector or director. The appointment needs the system-generated letter signed by the legal representative, both people's ID, and proof of the representative's authority. There is only one LEAR per organisation.

Can one organisation have two PICs?

It shouldn't. Duplicates are a known problem, which is why the wizard shows possible matches based on legal name and country. If you find a duplicate, report it to the Central Validation Service through Portal messaging and keep using the PIC with the validated history.

Why was my organisation's validation rejected?

The usual reasons are a legal name or address that doesn't match the registry extract, out-of-date VAT or registry documents, a declared status (non-profit, public body) that the statutes don't support, or no answer through the Participant Register. Correct the data under My Organisations, upload fresh documents and reply only through Portal messaging, because emails aren't accepted.
